claim: When the cost of carrying out self-repair is taken into account, LLM self-repair performance gains on HumanEval/APPS are often modest, vary a lot between data subsets, and are sometimes not present at all, across Code Llama, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4.
stance_target: That intrinsic self-correction/self-refinement without external verification is unreliable and can fail to improve over baseline
scope_conditions: Code generation on HumanEval and APPS; Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4
quoted_support: We find that when the cost of carrying out repair is taken into account, performance gains are often modest, vary a lot between subsets of the data, and are sometimes not present at all.

claim: Self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's own ability to provide feedback on its own code; using a stronger model to generate feedback (rather than the same model self-critiquing) produces substantially larger performance gains than intrinsic self-feedback.
stance_target: That self-correction requires external/stronger verification to be effective, i.e. intrinsic self-correction is capability-gated
scope_conditions: Code generation self-repair; feedback source ablation (self vs. stronger-model vs. human)
quoted_support: We hypothesize that this is because self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on its own code; using a stronger model to artificially boost the quality of the feedback, we observe substantially larger performance gains.

claim: Even for the strongest models tested (GPT-4), self-repair using the model's own feedback still lags far behind self-repair using human-provided feedback, in a small-scale human-feedback study.
stance_target: That model self-generated feedback is qualitatively weaker than external (human) feedback, independent of model scale/capability at the top end
scope_conditions: Small-scale human-participant feedback study with GPT-4
quoted_support: a small-scale study in which we provide GPT-4 with feedback from human participants suggests that even for the strongest models, self-repair still lags far behind what can be achieved with human-level debugging.

claim: This 2023 finding (self-repair gains are inconsistent and gated by feedback quality) predates and generalizes to a domain (code generation) distinct from NAS, establishing that a small model's self-refinement failing to improve or degrading proposals is directionally consistent with, not novel beyond, prior code-generation self-repair literature.
stance_target: Novelty of the target paper's feedback-degrades-proposals finding
scope_conditions: Cross-domain comparison: code self-repair (2023) vs. LLM-guided NAS feedback (2025-2026 target claim)
quoted_support: existing studies of self-repair have been limited in scope; in many settings, its efficacy thus remains poorly understood.
